objects.textPreview: Robot adaptation: learn what must change
Illustrative pick-and-lift example: a cube slips during execution.
The available grasp or motion is insufficient. Learn a different way to execute the task.
The mass or friction estimate is wrong. An existing movement may still succeed.
A failure alone does not identify the limitation; interaction must provide evidence.
The correction may belong to this encounter, this object or broader experience.

slides.titlePreview: A useful correction must have the right scope

objects.textPreview: A useful correction must have the right scope
Illustrative examples within the same pick-and-lift task.
A contact or pose error occurs only in this attempt. Revise the current state or physical estimate.
Repeated encounters reveal a wrong mass belief for this cube. Retain a correction for this object.
Whether to retain or generalize a correction is itself a learning problem.
Similar mismatches recur across objects. Reconsider the shared estimator, physical model or skill.
Top-down pick and lift. A fixed RL policy receives state and an estimated object mass.
From the initial RGB image Converted to weight for the policy
This setup isolates the context estimate; learning new movements is a longer-term direction.
Fixed material and density; predict mass from appearance. Test on held-out cube sizes within the sampled range.
Scope: one material; fixed density, friction and camera. Size interpolation only.
Next challenge: the same appearance can conceal a different mass.
One initial image → one mass estimate → a fixed policy → pick-and-lift execution.
Example run: 125.0 g actual → 121.24 g estimated; cube lifted and held.
Estimate fixed during execution; benefit over nominal context remains unmeasured.

slides.titlePreview: Next: turn response patterns into update decisions

objects.textPreview: Next: turn response patterns into update decisions
Build on completed motion grouping and controlled mass/friction response comparisons.
Two broad trajectory groups. Intended causal types unvalidated.
90 matched mass/friction trials; 7 observed response profiles.
Which evidence justifies changing an estimate, a model or a movement?
Changing actual physics is a different intervention from correcting the estimate.
Next: link observed patterns to useful update choices, then test those choices in execution.

slides.titlePreview: Then: test whether estimate updates help

objects.textPreview: Then: test whether estimate updates help
Proposed pilot: one cube appearance, varied mass. Keep friction and policy fixed.
Does accurate context help this policy? Can the available interaction reveal mass?
Initial estimate held fixed Interaction-updated estimate True mass supplied as a reference
Same interaction budget. Measure estimate error, task success and drops.
Train the update rule in simulation; at test time only the estimate changes.

objects.textPreview: Longer term: choose the correction and its scope
The fixed-policy study is one step toward improving both understanding and movement.
Wrong physical estimate? Missing physical factor? Insufficient movement capability?
A correction for this encounter? An object-specific belief? A change shared across future encounters?

slides.titlePreview: Failure-type discovery: behavior groups were not enough

objects.textPreview: Failure-type discovery: behavior groups were not enough
Completed exploration: identify meaningful failure types from recorded motion and pose.
Two broad groups of behavior. They did not establish the intended human-interpretable failure distinctions.
Causal explanations and known / unknown failure recognition remain unvalidated.
Motion / pose / force history → PCA + k-means → 2 candidate behavior groups
